title: System Architecture
description: Distributed systems in practice: sagas, events, bounded contexts and backends for frontends.
resumo: Sagas replace a distributed transaction with local steps and compensations — business actions, idempotent.
Kafka: durable, partitioned log; order only within a partition — key by aggregate id; consumers idempotent.
Bounded contexts: one model per context, each owning its data; no shared canonical model library.
BFF: one backend per client type, aggregating and formatting — business rules stay in the services.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an order touches three services with their own databases — orders, stock, payments. There is no single ACID transaction to roll everything back when the payment fails.

**Concept:** a saga splits the flow into local transactions and, when a step fails, runs compensations for the steps already done (refund the payment, release the stock). In choreography, each service reacts to events — simple, but the flow is implicit. In orchestration, a coordinator drives the steps — more visible and easier to monitor.

**How it works:** between steps the system is temporarily inconsistent (an order is "pending"), and the user interface must show that honestly.
examples.code:
Orchestrated saga "Place Order":
  1. Orders:   create order (PENDING)
  2. Stock:    reserve items        -- compensation: release the reservation
  3. Payments: charge the card      -- compensation: refund
  4. Orders:   confirm (PAID)

Failure at step 3 -> run the compensation of step 2 -> order CANCELLED
examples.interview_question: When would you apply the Saga pattern?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A compensation that "undoes" the record instead of the effect. Deleting the payment row does not give the customer their money back — the card was charged. A compensation is a business action (a refund), and it must be idempotent, because it can run more than once.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** new services keep needing to react to "order created", and every time the orders service gets a new HTTP call to make.

**Concept:** with a queue (RabbitMQ), each message goes to one consumer and is removed after processing — ideal for distributing work. With Kafka, events stay in a durable, partitioned log; several consumer groups read the same event independently and can replay history. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, so use the aggregate's id as the message key. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

**How it works:** the producer publishes facts ("OrderCreated"); each consumer decides what to do with them, and new consumers need no change to the producer.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between a queue (RabbitMQ) and an event log (Kafka)?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Publishing without a key (or with a random one). Events of the same order land on different partitions and can be processed out of order — "OrderPaid" before "OrderCreated". Use the order id as the key.

subsections.subtitle: Domain-Driven Design and Bounded Contexts
subsections.description: Drawing the boundaries of services and modules.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every change touches four services, which always deploy together — the boundaries were drawn in the wrong place.

**Concept:** split by business capability, not by technical layer. A bounded context is a boundary inside which one model and one language are consistent: "Product" in the catalog (description, photos) is not the same as "Product" in stock (quantity, warehouse). Contexts communicate through explicit contracts — APIs or events — and each one owns its data. Wrong boundaries produce the distributed monolith.

**How it works:** listen to the language: when the same word means different things to different teams, there are probably two contexts.
examples.interview_question: How do you define the boundaries between microservices?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: One shared "Product" class for every service (a canonical model in a common library). Every change to it forces every service to update and redeploy together, and each one carries fields it does not use.

subsections.subtitle: API Gateway and BFF
subsections.description: One entry point, and backends shaped for each client.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the mobile app needs a compact response from four services in one call, while the web app wants richer data — and one generic API serves neither well.

**Concept:** the API gateway handles cross-cutting concerns for every client — routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS. A BFF (Backend for Frontend) is a backend for one type of client: the mobile app gets compact, aggregated responses in one call, the web gets richer data, and each frontend team evolves its own BFF without affecting the others.

**How it works:** a BFF aggregates and shapes data; the business rules stay in the services behind it.
examples.interview_question: What is the advantage of a BFF for mobile and web apps?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Business rules in the BFFs. The discount rule is implemented in the mobile BFF and again in the web BFF, and after a few changes the two apps show different prices. Rules belong in the services; BFFs only aggregate and format.
examples.code:
WRONG: Mobile BFF and Web BFF both calculate the discount
       -> the same cart costs different amounts on each app

RIGHT: the pricing service calculates; both BFFs just display its result
